claims.text: An ML-augmented quantum-based model can explicitly incorporate scattering from approximately 1 wt.% oxygen and temperature-dependent electron–phonon coupling in bulk HfNbTaTiZr.
The proposed model will predict HfNbTaTiZr electrical conductivity more accurately than conventional defect-free analytical models over 0–200 K and 300–1200 K.
The modeled bulk HfNbTaTiZr specimen contains approximately 1 wt.% oxygen associated with interstitial defects.
Existing conductivity measurements from oxygen-containing HfNbTaTiZr can be used to train the proposed model.
Defect-scattering cross-sections, oxygen-induced potential landscapes, and temperature-dependent electron–phonon coupling are suitable model inputs.
Impurity and ionization scattering dominate conductivity in HfNbTaTiZr over nearly 0–200 K.
Intrinsic conduction dominates HfNbTaTiZr over 300–1200 K.
Electron–phonon interactions are significant in HfNbTaTiZr over 300–1200 K.
Interstitial oxygen modifies the electronic structure and creates scattering centers in HfNbTaTiZr.
Incorporating realistic oxygen-defect and temperature parameters will better capture oxygen-induced variations in carrier concentration and mobility.
Conventional analytical models for HfNbTaTiZr assume perfect, defect-free crystals and omit scattering and microstructural effects from 1 wt.% oxygen.
The proposed model will predict conductivity within 10% of experimental values.
The proposed model will improve prediction accuracy by more than 10% relative to conventional defect-free predictions.
The approach is restricted to HfNbTaTiZr specimens having oxygen contents near 1 wt.% and to 0–200 K and 300–1200 K.
The approximately 200–300 K interval is associated with extrinsic conduction effects.
The approach is not validated for specimens with substantially different impurity concentrations.
Limited training data and realistic defect-distribution complexity make the magnitude of the accuracy improvement uncertain.
A greater-than-10% conductivity error on held-out measurements from approximately 900–1200 K will falsify the model-accuracy hypothesis.
